lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Seeing how many, up to 5
lessons.intention: We are learning to see how many there are, up to 5, without counting.
criteria: I can say how many dots on a dice without counting.
I can show a number up to 5 on my fingers straight away.
I can spot 1 to 5 things in different patterns.

steps.start: Flash fingers for a second: how many? Show 3 a different way.
steps.teach: Show dice patterns 1 to 5 for two seconds each. Ask: how many? How did you know so fast? Then show the same number in a line, a triangle and a jumble: is it still 3? Talk about seeing 2 and 1 makes 3.
steps.practise: The "How many dots?" sheet: say how many in each box quickly, then write or circle the number.
steps.check: Flash 4 counters in a jumble for two seconds: how many? Then 5 in a dice pattern.

lessons.home: Play a quick dice game: roll and say how many without counting the dots.
lessons.vocab: how many, the same, dice, pattern, fingers
lessons.understand: How did you know there were 4 without counting?
lessons.lookFor: Sees parts (2 and 2, or 3 and 1), or recognises the pattern; doesn't point and count each dot.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: What numbers are made of, to 10
lessons.intention: We are learning that a number can be split into two parts in different ways.
criteria: I can split 5 into two parts, like 4 and 1 or 3 and 2.
I can use a ten frame to show a number to 10.
I can say what a number is made of.

steps.start: Count to 10 and back with fingers. Hold up 5 fingers: how many on each hand could make 5?
steps.teach: Put 5 counters in a line. Push some to one side: 3 and 2 make 5. Move one more: 4 and 1 make 5. Do the same with 6 to 10 on a ten frame (an egg box with 10 holes works). Say each part: 7 is 5 and 2.
steps.practise: The "What's inside the number?" sheet: count the two colours in each frame and write the parts.
steps.check: Show 6 counters: hide some under a cup. How many are hiding? Ask for two different ways to make 6.

lessons.home: Split 5 or 6 small toys between two hands or two boxes in as many ways as you can.
lessons.vocab: part, whole, makes, split, ten frame
lessons.understand: Is 4 and 1 the same amount as 3 and 2? How do you know?
lessons.lookFor: Knows both make 5: the whole stays the same however it's split.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Number bonds to 5
lessons.intention: We are learning to know the pairs that make 5, and to take away within 5.
criteria: I can say the pairs that make 5 without counting.
I can work out how many are left when some are taken away.
I can find the missing part of 5.

steps.start: Hold up 5 fingers, fold some down: how many up, how many down?
steps.teach: Use 5 counters and a cup. Hide some: if 2 are showing, how many are hiding? Say the pair together: 2 and 3 make 5. Then take away: 5 apples, eat 1, how many left? Practise until the pairs come quickly.
steps.check: Ask quickly: 1 and? 3 and? 5 take away 2? 0 and?

lessons.home: At snack time: 5 grapes, eat some, how many are left? How many did you eat?
lessons.vocab: add, take away, makes, left, pair
lessons.understand: If 4 and 1 make 5, what is 5 take away 1?
lessons.lookFor: Sees the link: the same pair works both ways, so they don't need to count.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Number bonds to 10, and doubles
lessons.intention: We are learning some pairs that make 10, and doubles up to double 5.
criteria: I can find the missing part of 10 on a ten frame.
I know some pairs that make 10, like 5 and 5, and 7 and 3.
I can say doubles up to double 5.

steps.start: Clap and count to 10. Show 10 fingers, fold 3 down: how many are still up?
steps.teach: Fill a ten frame with 7 counters: how many empty spaces? 7 and 3 make 10. Do 9, 6 and 8 the same way. Then doubles: put the same number on each side of a mirror or a folded paper: double 3 is 6.
steps.check: Show a frame with 8: how many more to make 10? Then ask double 4 and double 5.

lessons.home: Count socks into pairs; play "make 10" with fingers in the car or at the shop.
lessons.vocab: ten frame, make 10, double, the same, pair
lessons.understand: Why is double 5 the same as 5 and 5?
lessons.lookFor: Knows doubling means two groups the same size.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: More, fewer or the same, up to 10
lessons.intention: We are learning to compare two groups and say which has more, fewer or the same.
criteria: I can say which group has more.
I can say which group has fewer.
I can tell when two groups are the same, by matching them up.

steps.start: Put 3 spoons and 5 forks out: which is more? How can we tell?
steps.teach: Line two groups up one to one, like cups and saucers: the group with extra has more, the other has fewer. Make them the same by adding or taking away. Do it with numbers too: 7 is more than 4.
steps.practise: The "More, fewer or the same" sheet.
steps.check: Show 6 and 8 counters in jumbled heaps: which has more? Ask them to check by lining them up.

lessons.home: At tea time: are there more cups or more plates? How many more?
lessons.vocab: more, fewer, the same, most, fewest, match
lessons.understand: A big heap of tiny buttons and a small heap of big blocks: which has more? How can you be sure?
lessons.lookFor: Counts or matches them; knows size of the things doesn't change how many.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Odd and even, and sharing fairly
lessons.intention: We are learning to spot odd and even numbers by making pairs, and to share things fairly.
criteria: I can put things into pairs and see if there's one left over.
I know that even numbers make pairs with none left.
I can share things fairly between two.

steps.start: Count pairs of socks or shoes in twos: 2, 4, 6.
steps.teach: Make pairs with 6 counters: none left over, so 6 is even. Try 7: one is left on its own, so 7 is odd. Then share 8 sweets between two teddies: one for you, one for you. Are they fair?
steps.check: Give 9 counters: odd or even? How do you know? Share 6 between two plates.

lessons.home: Sort the washing into pairs of socks; share fruit fairly between two people.
lessons.vocab: odd, even, pair, share, fair, left over
lessons.understand: If you share 7 sweets between two people, is it fair? Why not?
lessons.lookFor: Explains that one is left over, so 7 is odd; links odd numbers to not sharing fairly between two.

lessons.subject: Maths
lessons.title: Counting past 20
lessons.intention: We are learning to count past 20 and see the pattern in the numbers.
criteria: I can count to 30 and beyond.
I can say what comes next after 29.
I can see that numbers repeat 1 to 9 in each ten.

steps.start: Count to 20 together, clapping, then whisper on to 25.
steps.teach: Write 1 to 40 in rows of ten (a number track or a 100 square). Point to the pattern: 21, 22, 23 sound like 1, 2, 3 with twenty in front. What comes after 29? Count objects in tens: 10, 20, 30.
steps.check: Ask them to count on from 18 to 32. Then: what comes after 39?

lessons.home: Count steps, stairs or cars out loud past 20 together.
lessons.vocab: count on, twenty, thirty, next, before, after, tens
lessons.understand: What comes after 29, and how do you know?
lessons.lookFor: Knows the tens change (twenty to thirty) and the ones start again at 0.
